summary: Specifies a way to carry long addresses in the HOST-PORT part of FTP's data port command, so FTP can work with next-generation IP alternatives and perhaps other transports besides TCP. It is experimental. It was replaced by RFC 1639.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes extended FTP commands for data connections with longer addresses. The LPRT and LPSV formats include the address family and the lengths of the host and port addresses.

questions: ftp operation over big address records
subtitle: An experimental FTP command format for longer host and transport addresses.

tldr.problem: FTP's PORT command uses a fixed-size host and port representation, while other address families or transports may require longer values.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines LPRT with explicit address-family and length fields, and LPSV for passive transfers using a long address. It also defines reply code 521 for unsupported address families.
tldr.outcome: The memo proposes a flexible experimental convention for FTP data connections. RFC 1639 later replaced it.

today: RFC 1545 is Experimental and was replaced by RFC 1639. It proposed long-address commands for FTP data connections.

sections.title: Why FTP Needs a Longer Address Format
sections.content:
The FTP PORT command identifies a data connection using a 32-bit host address and a 16-bit TCP port address, represented as comma-separated decimal fields. RFC 1545 proposes a different convention for longer addresses and for transport interfaces other than TCP.

The memo is an Experimental Protocol and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The original PORT format has fixed-size fields for a host and a TCP port. This proposal adds a format that can describe addresses of different lengths.

sections.title: LPRT and LPSV Commands
sections.content:
LPRT carries an address-family value, a host-address length and its fields, then a port-address length and its fields. Each value is represented as unsigned decimal numbers separated by commas. The address-family value identifies an Internet-layer protocol.

LPSV asks the server to listen for the data connection and return its long address information. Reply code 228 indicates entry into long passive mode. The RFC adds reply code 521 for a supported command with an unsupported requested address family.
sections.plainLanguage: LPRT tells the server which address family and address fields to use. LPSV lets the server provide its own long address while waiting for a data connection.

sections.title: Reason for the Length Fields
sections.content:
The RFC says an explicit address family lets one FTP implementation support several proposed Internet-layer protocols. A host-address length is needed because some alternatives use variable-length addresses. A port-address length may also help with transports whose selectors or port numbers exceed the TCP port size.

The memo concludes that the convention is simple and extensible for the Internet Protocol alternatives under discussion and potentially for other protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The fields make the command adaptable to different address formats. The RFC also considers that some transports may need longer port values.

sections.title: Status of the Proposal
sections.content: RFC 1545 defines an experimental convention and says it is not an Internet standard. The unit metadata identifies RFC 1639 as its replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: This was an experimental FTP proposal. RFC 1639 later replaced it.

references.text: Postel, J. and J. Reynolds, "File Transfer Protocol", STD 9, RFC 959, October 1985.
